title: Five vowels, one sound each
rule: a = ah · e = eh · i = ee · o = oh · u = oo — always, and every one is said · stress: second-to-last syllable, unless an accent says otherwise
hook: English vowels are chaos: the a in cat, car, cake and about are four different sounds. Spanish has five, and each only ever makes one sound. Nothing is silent — a final -e is always said. Stress is just as tidy: words ending in a vowel, n or s lean on the second-to-last syllable, everything else on the last — and when a word breaks that rule, it wears a written accent to tell you. So you can read any Spanish word aloud, even one you've never met.

examples.hint: ends in r, so the stress falls on the last syllable
the accent pulls the stress to the end

examples.prompt: Now read it cold: Quiero comer
examples.hint: qu = k; comer ends in r, so stress on the end

title: j (and g before e, i) is a throaty h
rule: j = a breathy h from the back of the throat · g before e or i = the same sound · g before a, o, u = hard g · gu before e/i keeps it hard
hook: Say the h in "hello", then scrape it a little further back — like clearing your throat gently, or the ch in Scottish "loch". That's the Spanish j. Respelled here as plain h, because that's close enough to be understood everywhere. The letter g does it too, but only before e or i — the same trick as c. The x in México and Oaxaca is the same sound, an old spelling that stuck.

examples.hint: ju = hoo, sliding into the a
the u is silent — it only keeps the g hard
the x is a j sound here

examples.prompt: Now read it cold: Me gusta el jugo
examples.hint: g before u stays hard, j is h

title: h is always silent
rule: h = nothing at all · except in ch, which is "ch" as in church
hook: The Spanish h is pure decoration — a fossil of Latin spelling. Pretend it isn't there. Hola is OH-lah, hotel is oh-TEL. The only time it does anything is next to a c, where ch sounds exactly like English church.

examples.hint: stress on the end — it finishes in l
the h in the middle vanishes too
ch = church; and the final -e is said

examples.prompt: Now read it cold: Hasta ahora

title: ñ = ny
rule: ñ = the ny in canyon · it's a separate letter, not an n with decoration
hook: You already make this sound in canyon and onion. The squiggle matters: año is a year, ano is an anus. Say Happy New Year carefully.

examples.hint: never drop the tilde on this one

examples.prompt: Now read it cold: Feliz año
examples.hint: z is an s in Latin America

title: ll and y are the same sound
rule: ll = y as in yes · y = the same · y on its own ("and") = ee
hook: Across most of Latin America ll and y are pronounced identically — a y as in yes, sometimes buzzing towards the j in jam. (In Argentina and Uruguay both become sh: YAH-moh becomes SHAH-moh.) It's never an English l.

examples.prompt: Now read it cold: Ella llega mañana

title: r is a tap, rr is a roll
rule: single r between vowels = a quick tap (the tt in American "butter") · rr, or r at the start of a word = a roll · respelled here as r and rr
hook: Say "butter" fast, American-style: that flick of the tongue in the middle is the Spanish r. Keep flicking and you get rr. It changes words: pero is "but", perro is "dog"; caro is "expensive", carro is "car". An r at the very start of a word is always rolled.

examples.prompt: Which one is "expensive": caro or carro?

examples.hint: a starting r is always rolled

examples.prompt: Now read it cold: El perro es caro

title: c before e/i, and z, are s
rule: Latin America: ce, ci and z = s · c before a, o, u = k · qu = k
hook: In Spain ce, ci and z are a lisped th; across Latin America they're simply s. So cinco, zapato and casa all have a sound you already own. And just like in Italian, the vowel after the c decides: before a, o, u it's a hard k. To get a k before e or i, Spanish writes qu — the u is silent.

examples.hint: qu = k, the u is silent

examples.prompt: Now read it cold: Quiero cerveza
examples.hint: and v sounds like b — see the next bridge

title: b and v are the same sound
rule: b = v = a b sound · between vowels it softens, lips barely touching · respelled here as b
hook: Spanish speakers can't hear a difference between b and v, and they have to learn which to write the way English kids learn their/there. Say both as b. Between vowels the lips don't quite close, so it's a soft, breathy b — but never the English v with teeth on lip.

examples.prompt: Now read it cold: Vivo en Bogotá
examples.hint: the accent puts the stress on the end

title: -tion → -ción
rule: English -tion  →  Spanish -ción (always with the accent, always feminine: la …)
hook: Here's your first thousand words. Almost every English word ending in -tion exists in Spanish with -ción instead. They came from the same Latin word; English softened the t into "sh", Latin American Spanish turned it into a plain s. Say it -SYOHN, stress on the end — that's what the accent is for.

examples.hint: Spanish rarely doubles a consonant — one t

title: -ity → -idad
rule: English -ity  →  Spanish -idad (always feminine: la …)
hook: Swap the -ity for -idad, put the stress on the very end, and you're done. Spanish doesn't like double consonants, so if the English has one, keep just one letter.

examples.hint: It's a = Es una (una because -idad is feminine)

title: -ous → -oso
rule: English -ous  →  Spanish -oso (-osa when it describes a woman or a feminine word)
hook: An easy swap that unlocks a whole family of describing words. And since they end in -o, they agree like any other: a famous man is famoso, a famous woman is famosa.

examples.hint: an i slips in before the -oso
she is = es; a woman, so -a

title: -ly → -mente
rule: English -ly  →  Spanish -mente, stuck onto the -a form of the adjective
hook: English adds -ly to make an adverb; Spanish adds -mente ("with a mind": calmly = with a calm mind). Glue it onto the adjective — and if the adjective ends in -o, switch it to -a first. If it ends in anything else, just add -mente.

examples.prompt: Now build it — "Finally I can eat"
examples.hint: I can = puedo, to eat = comer

title: -ic / -ical → -ico
rule: English -ic or -ical  →  Spanish -ico, with the stress pulled back (written with an accent)
hook: Add an -o, then lean hard on the syllable before -ico — that's why these words almost always carry an accent: fan-TAS-ti-co. Make it -ica for a woman or a feminine word.

title: -ive → -ivo
rule: English -ive  →  Spanish -ivo (-iva for feminine)
hook: Swap the silent English -e for a spoken -o. That's the whole trick.

examples.prompt: Now build it — "I'm very creative" (a woman speaking)

title: -ant / -ent → -ante / -ente
rule: English -ant  →  -ante · English -ent  →  -ente
hook: Just add an -e on the end. These are the same for men and women — one less thing to think about.

title: s + consonant → es-
rule: an English word starting s + consonant  →  Spanish puts an e in front: es-
hook: Spanish can't start a word with s and then another consonant — it physically has to say a vowel first. Listen to a Spanish speaker say "eSpanish" and you've heard this rule. So special becomes especial. Often another bridge is waiting at the end of the word too.

title: -ize → -izar
rule: English verbs in -ize / -ise  →  Spanish -izar ("to …")
hook: A big family of verbs, all regular -ar verbs, so they behave exactly like hablar. Say -ee-SAHR. Careful with realize: realizar means to carry out. "To realize" is darse cuenta.

examples.prompt: Now build it — "I have to organize it"
examples.hint: I have to = Tengo que; it = lo, stuck on the end

title: -ary → -ario, -ory → -orio
rule: English -ary  →  -ario · English -ory  →  -orio
hook: Add the vowels back. Stress falls on the a or o: ne-ce-SA-rio, la-bo-ra-TO-rio.

title: -ence → -encia, -ance → -ancia
rule: English -ence  →  -encia · English -ance  →  -ancia
hook: Swap the silent -e for -ia, and say it -EN-syah. These are all feminine.

title: ph → f
rule: English ph  →  Spanish f
hook: Spanish spells sounds the way they sound. A ph is an f, so it's written f.

examples.hint: ph → f, and add -o; the stress jumps to te-LE

examples.prompt: Now build it — "I want a photo"
examples.hint: una, even though it ends in -o — it's short for fotografía

title: th → t
rule: English th  →  Spanish t
hook: Spanish has no th sound in its spelling, so Greek and Latin words that English writes with th come out with a plain t.

examples.hint: plus -o; stress on the first syllable

examples.prompt: Now build it — "I want to go to the theatre"

title: -ble stays -ble
rule: English -ble  →  Spanish -ble, but every letter is said: -bleh
hook: The freebie. The spelling barely changes — the work is in the mouth. Say the final e (-bleh), and put the stress on the syllable before it: po-SI-ble, ho-RRI-ble.
